title: Exome Yield, mtDNA Heteroplasmy, Secondary Findings and Testing Children
summary: Learn what an exome and the mitochondrial genome are, why heteroplasmy means a negative blood mtDNA test can miss disease, how often exome sequencing finds a diagnosis, what ACMG secondary findings are, and why predictive testing of children for adult-onset conditions is deferred.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 72 Hits 14 (mtDNA 16,569 bp, maternal inheritance, heteroplasmy), 15 (exome size, variant burden, diagnostic yield) and 16 (ACMG incidental/secondary findings list; predictive testing of children) and Exam Traps 4 (heteroplasmy and blood testing), 5 (exome yield) and 6 (testing children for adult-onset disorders). Checked against Govers 2021 and Stitziel 2011 and Clark 2018 (Europe PMC full text), the Mitochondrial Medicine Society 2015 consensus, the ASHG 2015 points to consider and the ACMG 2021 secondary-findings update, Green 2013 and the ACMG SF v3.3 list (all read via a page-fetch tool). The reviewer’s “~25 diseases” is the 2013 list; the current v3.3 list has 84 genes (rv-acmg-sf-list-current). The reviewer’s “genuine psychosocial harm” and “<18” are not taught; ASHG 2015 gives autonomy as the reason and found no evidence of significant psychosocial harm (rv-predictive-testing-children-rationale). Exome size and variant counts are taught from the sources as approximate (rv-exome-size-variant-count). The reviewer’s “VUS results are a major counseling challenge” is not taught. Guidance is US-based (rv-genomic-guidance-us-only).

objectives: Describe the exome and the mitochondrial genome (16,569 bp, circular, 37 genes, maternal inheritance).
Explain how heteroplasmy and tissue variation can make a blood mtDNA test negative, and name better specimens and methods.
State the approximate diagnostic yield of exome sequencing in children and why a nondiagnostic exome does not exclude a genetic cause.
Define ACMG secondary findings and state the current list version and size.
Explain why predictive testing of children for adult-onset conditions is usually deferred.

scenes.title: Three negative-sounding answers
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three requests reach a molecular genetics desk — (1) the parents of a healthy 9-year-old whose father has Huntington disease ask for predictive testing now; (2) a child with developmental delay has a nondiagnostic exome, and the parents ask whether a genetic cause is now excluded; (3) an adult with a suspected mitochondrial disorder has a negative mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) test on blood, and the clinician asks whether mitochondrial disease is ruled out. Question token: “Test now? Excluded? Ruled out?”

cues.text: Three requests reach the genetics desk. Parents of a healthy nine-year-old, whose father has Huntington disease, want the child tested now.
A child with developmental delay has a nondiagnostic exome. Is a genetic cause now excluded?
And an adult with a suspected mitochondrial disorder has a negative mitochondrial DNA test on blood. Is it ruled out?

scenes.title: Two small genomes inside the big one
scenes.altText: Four cards. Exome: almost all known exons plus several hundred intronic nucleotides at exon ends, roughly 2% of the genome in one meta-analysis (the reviewer gives ~1.5%; the figure depends on how the target is defined). Variants: one review reports typically 15,000–20,000 variants per exome, depending on the exome target and ancestry, filtered down toward a single causal variant. mtDNA: a circular, double-stranded 16,569-bp molecule with 37 genes (13 polypeptides, 22 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs). Inheritance: mtDNA comes from the mother because paternal mitochondria are eliminated; homoplasmy means all copies carry a variant, heteroplasmy means mutant and normal copies coexist, and dysfunction needs a threshold level of mutant mtDNA.

cues.text: An exome is almost all known exons, plus some intronic bases at their edges. A large pediatric meta-analysis describes it as roughly two percent of the genome.

Even that small slice holds thousands of variants: one review reports typically fifteen to twenty thousand per exome, depending on the target and ancestry. Filtering narrows them toward one causal variant.
Mitochondrial DNA is a separate, circular, double-stranded genome of sixteen thousand five hundred sixty-nine base pairs, with thirty-seven genes.

It is inherited from the mother, because paternal mitochondria are eliminated. Mutant and normal copies can coexist, called heteroplasmy, and a threshold level of mutant DNA is needed before the cell fails.

scenes.title: Heteroplasmy: why blood can miss it
scenes.altText: Heteroplasmy card: a heteroplasmic mother passes a variable share of mutant mtDNA because of the germline bottleneck; after fertilisation, random partitioning means mutant load can differ between tissues of one person, and the threshold differs by tissue energy demand. Specimen card (Mitochondrial Medicine Society 2015 consensus): low heteroplasmy or tissue-specific variants can be missed in blood; urine heteroplasmy analysis can be more informative than blood, especially for the common m.3243A>G (MELAS) variant; massively parallel sequencing of the whole mtDNA genome is preferred over testing a few point mutations; skeletal muscle or liver are preferred tissue sources for mtDNA genome sequencing when available, and biopsy is used when DNA testing cannot confirm the diagnosis. Token: more than 1,400 nuclear genes affect mitochondrial function, and mtDNA variants can arise de novo.

cues.text: A heteroplasmic mother passes on a variable share of mutant copies, because only a small number of mitochondrial DNA molecules pass through the germline bottleneck. After fertilisation, copies are split at random, so one person’s tissues can carry different mutant loads.

That is why blood can mislead. The consensus statement of the Mitochondrial Medicine Society warns that low-level or tissue-specific variants can be missed in blood, and that urine can be more informative, especially for the common MELAS variant m.3243A>G.

Sequence the whole mitochondrial genome by next-generation sequencing, not a short list of point mutations. Skeletal muscle or liver are preferred sources when available, and biopsy is used when DNA testing cannot confirm the diagnosis.
And mitochondrial disease is not only maternal: more than fourteen hundred nuclear genes affect mitochondria, and mitochondrial DNA variants can also arise new in a child.

lines: Whole-mtDNA NGS, not a few spots
Muscle or liver; biopsy if needed

scenes.title: Exome yield and secondary findings
scenes.altText: Yield card (Clark 2018 meta-analysis, 37 studies, 20,068 children with suspected genetic disease): pooled diagnostic utility of exome sequencing 0.36 (95% CI 0.33–0.40), genome sequencing 0.41 (0.34–0.48), chromosomal microarray 0.10; trio testing roughly doubled the odds of diagnosis compared with singleton testing (OR 2.04). Secondary findings card (ACMG): variants actively sought in a defined gene list, unrelated to the test indication; 2013 list of 57 genes in about two dozen conditions, to be reported regardless of age; the 2021 update allows patients to opt out and says variants of uncertain significance are not returned as secondary findings; the 2025 v3.3 list has 84 genes. Hook answers: (1) defer predictive Huntington testing until the child can decide; (2) a nondiagnostic exome does not exclude a genetic cause; (3) a negative blood mtDNA test does not rule out mitochondrial disease.

cues.text: How often does an exome find the answer? A meta-analysis of thirty-seven studies in children with suspected genetic disease found a pooled diagnostic rate of about thirty-six percent for exomes, and forty-one percent for genomes.
Testing the child together with both parents, a trio, about doubled the odds of a diagnosis. So a nondiagnostic exome leaves the question open.

Secondary findings are different: variants the laboratory deliberately searches for in a defined gene list, unrelated to why the test was ordered. The 2013 list had fifty-seven genes; the 2025 version has eighty-four, patients may opt out, and uncertain variants are not returned as secondary findings.
Back to the hook. Defer the child’s Huntington test. The nondiagnostic exome does not exclude a genetic cause. And the negative blood test does not rule out mitochondrial disease.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Negative blood mtDNA test = no mitochondrial disease” (✓ heteroplasmy differs by tissue; consider urine, muscle or liver, whole-mtDNA sequencing and nuclear genes); “A nondiagnostic exome excludes a genetic cause” (✓ pooled exome yield in children about 36%); “Test children now for adult-onset disease” (✓ defer to adulthood unless an intervention is appropriate in childhood).

cues.text: Trap one: a negative mitochondrial test on blood rules out disease. No: mutant load differs between tissues, so consider urine, muscle or liver, and remember nuclear genes.
Trap two: a nondiagnostic exome excludes a genetic cause. No: in children, exomes find the diagnosis in only about a third of cases.
Trap three: test children now for an adult-onset disease. No: defer predictive testing to adulthood unless something can be done in childhood.

scenes.title: Index, batteries, sealed letter
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The exome is the INDEX of a huge book: a search that finds nothing does not mean the book is clean. mtDNA is MOM’S BATTERIES: every tissue gets its own mix of good and bad cells, so test the device that is failing. Adult-onset results in a child are a SEALED LETTER: wait until the reader can choose to open it.” Tokens: index = exome · batteries = mtDNA · sealed letter = predictive testing in children. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the exome is the index of a huge book, so an empty search does not prove the book is clean. Mitochondrial DNA is mom’s batteries, mixed differently in each tissue, so test the device that is failing. And adult-onset news for a child is a sealed letter: wait until the reader can choose.

Where it breaks: an exome reads the coding text itself, not a pointer to it; mitochondrial disease can also come from nuclear genes, not from mom; and the letter may be opened early when something can be done in childhood.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Exome ~36% yield in children · blood can miss heteroplasmy → urine, tissue, whole mtDNA”, “ACMG secondary findings: sought list, 84 genes (v3.3) · defer adult-onset testing in children”.

cues.text: A nondiagnostic exome or a negative blood mitochondrial DNA test does not exclude genetic disease, secondary findings come from a deliberately searched and regularly updated gene list, and predictive testing of children for adult-onset conditions is deferred unless something can be done in childhood.

props.label: Exome ~36% in children · blood misses heteroplasmy → urine, tissue
Secondary findings: sought list (84 genes) · defer adult-onset tests

explanation.what: Plain language: an exome test reads the small part of our DNA that codes for proteins, and it finds the answer in only about a third of children tested for a suspected genetic disease. Mitochondria carry their own tiny circle of DNA, passed down from the mother, and a mix of healthy and faulty copies can differ from one tissue to another, so a blood test can miss it. Labs may also deliberately look for a fixed list of genes where acting on a result is likely to reduce illness and death, even if unrelated to the test reason. And children are usually not tested for diseases that only start in adulthood. Scientific terms: exome sequencing (ES/WES), genome sequencing (GS/WGS), chromosomal microarray (CMA), trio vs singleton testing, variant filtering, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), homoplasmy, heteroplasmy, threshold effect, germline bottleneck, m.3243A>G (MELAS), secondary vs incidental findings, ACMG SF list, opt-out, variant of uncertain significance (VUS), predictive (presymptomatic) testing.
explanation.why: An exome captures only exons, and even then each one holds thousands of variants that must be filtered, so many causal variants are missed or not recognised. Heteroplasmic mtDNA is shared out at random through the germline bottleneck and again during development, so mutant load and its threshold differ between tissues. Secondary findings are reported because the listed genes have a high likelihood of reducing illness and death when acted on. Deferring adult-onset predictive testing lets the child make that decision later.
explanation.measure: Exome: roughly 2% of the genome; typically about 15,000–20,000 variants per exome (target- and ancestry-dependent); pooled diagnostic utility in children 0.36 (genome 0.41, microarray 0.10); trio about twice the odds of diagnosis of singleton. mtDNA: 16,569 bp, 37 genes (13 polypeptides, 22 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs); prefer whole-mtDNA massively parallel sequencing; urine can be more informative than blood for m.3243A>G; muscle or liver preferred tissue sources; biopsy if DNA testing cannot confirm. ACMG SF: 57 genes in 2013, 84 genes in v3.3 (2025); opt-out allowed; VUS not returned as secondary findings.
explanation.differs: Secondary findings (deliberately sought in a defined list) vs incidental findings (found accidentally); homoplasmy vs heteroplasmy; blood vs urine or affected tissue for mtDNA; mtDNA-encoded vs nuclear-encoded mitochondrial disease; predictive testing for adult-onset conditions (defer) vs testing when childhood intervention exists (justified).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the next step after a negative blood mtDNA test with a classic phenotype, how to counsel after a nondiagnostic exome, what the ACMG secondary-findings list is, and how to respond when parents request Huntington testing of a healthy child.

questions.stem: An adult has features suggesting MELAS. Testing of blood for m.3243A>G is negative. What is the best next step?

options.text: Test another specimen such as urine or muscle, ideally with whole-mtDNA sequencing
options.rationale: Correct. Heteroplasmy differs between tissues, low levels can be missed in blood, and urine can be more informative for m.3243A>G; whole-mtDNA sequencing is preferred, and muscle or liver are preferred tissues.

options.text: Test the father’s blood for the variant
options.rationale: Incorrect. mtDNA is inherited from the mother; paternal mitochondria are eliminated.

options.text: Report that mitochondrial disease is excluded
options.rationale: Incorrect. A negative blood result does not exclude tissue-specific or low-level variants, or nuclear-gene causes.

options.text: Repeat the same blood test in one week
options.rationale: Incorrect. The problem is the specimen and the narrow test, not timing; another tissue and broader sequencing are needed.

questions.stem: A child’s exome sequencing is nondiagnostic. The parents ask whether a genetic cause has been excluded. What is the best response?

options.text: No; exome sequencing finds a diagnosis in only about a third of children tested
options.rationale: Correct. A meta-analysis found pooled diagnostic utility of 0.36 for exome sequencing in children with suspected genetic disease.

options.text: Yes; the exome covers all disease-causing variants
options.rationale: Incorrect. The exome is roughly 2% of the genome, and many diagnoses are missed.

options.text: The thousands of variants found indicate a laboratory error
options.rationale: Incorrect. Thousands of variants per exome (typically about 15,000–20,000 in one review) are expected.

options.text: Ask the laboratory to report all variants of uncertain significance as secondary findings
options.rationale: Incorrect. Under ACMG guidance, variants of uncertain significance are not returned as secondary findings.

questions.stem: The father of a healthy 10-year-old has Huntington disease. The parents ask for predictive testing of the child. What does the ASHG 2015 guidance recommend?

options.text: Encourage deferring testing until adulthood, so the child can make the decision
options.rationale: Correct. ASHG advises deferring predictive testing for adult-onset conditions unless a clinical intervention is appropriate in childhood.

options.text: Test now, because earlier knowledge always helps
options.rationale: Incorrect. Without an intervention in childhood, testing removes the child’s own future choice.

options.text: Test now, because the ACMG secondary-findings list requires it
options.rationale: Incorrect. Secondary findings apply to exome or genome sequencing ordered for another reason; they do not mandate targeted predictive testing.

options.text: Test now but keep the result secret until the child turns 18
options.rationale: Incorrect. Testing still takes the decision away from the child; the guidance is to defer testing itself.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 72 Hit 16 says the “ACMG incidental-findings list covers ~25 diseases”. That matches the original 2013 list (Green 2013: 57 genes in about two dozen conditions, called incidental findings and with no patient opt-out). ACMG now calls them secondary findings (variants actively sought in a defined list), allows patients to opt out (2021 update), updates the list each year, and the ACMG SF v3.3 list (Lee 2025) has 84 genes (counted from its Table 1). The lesson teaches the current list and names the 2013 figure as historical (register flag rv-acmg-sf-list-current).

Ch. 72 Hit 16 and Trap 6 discourage predictive testing of children “<18” for adult-onset disorders because of “no medical benefit in childhood, but genuine psychosocial harm”. The ASHG 2015 points-to-consider statement (Botkin 2015) does advise deferring such testing to adulthood unless a clinical intervention is appropriate in childhood, but it names no fixed age, bases deferral on letting the child make their own decision later, and states that the limited research to date has not found evidence of significant psychosocial harms in children. The lesson teaches the ASHG wording and does not teach psychosocial harm as an established finding (register flag rv-predictive-testing-children-rationale).

Ch. 72 Hit 15 gives the exome as ~1.5% of the genome with 20,000–30,000 variants per exome and a diagnostic yield of 25–50%. Clark 2018 describes exome sequencing as covering approximately 2% of the genome and reports pooled diagnostic utility of 0.36 (95% CI 0.33–0.40) for exomes in children; Stitziel 2011 reports typically 15,000–20,000 variants per exome, varying with the exome target definition and ancestry. These figures depend on capture design, population and indication, so the lesson teaches the sourced values as approximate (register flag rv-exome-size-variant-count).

The secondary-findings and paediatric-testing guidance taught here comes from US professional societies (ACMG, ASHG) and the Mitochondrial Medicine Society. Philippine rules or professional guidance on genomic secondary findings and predictive testing of minors are not covered and were not checked (register flag rv-genomic-guidance-us-only).
